transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Park (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (Redwood CSM); Maya Singh (Head of ML - Acme), Tom Reynolds (CTO), Sara Lee (Infra), Devon Kim (PM)

[00:00] Jamie: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, i'll kick off quick. agenda — scope the poc, success criteria, what you'll bring for sizing/benchmarks, and decide what deployment modes we should exercise (hosted / dedicated / private). sound good?
[00:12] Maya: yeah that works, thanks Jamie. quick ask up front, we're evaluating where to run inference: want to see cost/latency tradeoffs and security fit.
[00:22] Tom: and timeline — ideally a POC we can finish within 4–6 weeks so execs can greenlight next quarter.
[00:30] Jamie: got it. i'll hand to Luis for technical framing and what we recommend for benchmarks.
[00:35] Luis: cool. hi all. quick note — i'll suggest we run a focused 2-week hosted benchmark first so we can get apples-to-apples numbers for latency, throughput, and cost. then if needed we can spin up a dedicated pool and a private deployment for deeper network/security testing.
[00:50] Nina: adding that we'll also share our evaluation harness and a sample prompsheet — forgive my voice, auto-transcript sometimes mangles words.
[00:58] Devon: yeah the harness would be great. our ML team wants p95 latency under 250ms for short chat flows and throughput of ~600 requests / minute during peak.
[01:12] Luis: noted. can you confirm typical request size (avg tokens) and streaming vs non-streaming?
[01:20] Maya: average prompt ~90 tokens, responses ~140 tokens. most use-cases use streaming for chat, but we also have a few synchronous batch endpoints for content gen.
[01:30] Jamie: awesome — that's helpful. so initial success criteria we heard: p95 latency < 250ms (streaming where possible), throughput ~600 r/min, cost target roughly <$0.015 per 1k tokens (ballpark — we can refine). also quality/regression threshold: less than 5% drop vs current baseline on our eval set.
[01:52] Tom: that cost target is aggressive; how do you typically hit it? dedicated/quantization/kv-cache?
[02:00] Luis: exactly — main levers are dedicated capacity (reserved GPUs), mixed precision/quantized weights, and prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts. hosted can be optimized too but dedicated gives you predictable unit economics at scale.
[02:15] Sara: quick security note — we require SOC2, SSO (SAML/OIDC), audit logs, and bring-your-own-kms (we use AWS KMS). for private, we'd need VPC peering and options for on-prem if later.
[02:30] Jamie: yes we've got SOC 2 report and SSO + RBAC support. for KMS we support customer-managed keys in both Dedicated and Private offerings; hosted can integrate with external KMS via HSM connectors for enterprise accounts. i'll share the security pack.
[02:45] Maya: great. can you also explain routing/fallbacks? if we go dedicated and capacity spikes, do requests fall back to hosted?
[02:55] Luis: yes, there's smart routing — policy-based. you can prefer dedicated, then failover to hosted or smaller model variants. we also support canary rollouts and automatic fallback for latency SLO violations. sometimes transcript shows "Redwood Dedicate" — that's us, sorry.
[03:12] Devon: on benchmarks, what metrics should we gather?
[03:18] Luis: baseline p50/p95/p99, token throughput (tokens/s), cost per 1k tokens, GPU utilization, tail latency under load, memory/KV-cache hit rates, and model output quality measured by your eval set (accuracy, BLEU-ish metrics or classification accuracy depending). also error rates and cold-start times for new model versions.
[03:40] Maya: for model versions — we use an internal repo and often pin to exact checkpoints. how does Redwood handle model rollouts?
[03:48] Jamie: we support version pinning and gradual rollouts (canary/A-B) with traffic split and automatic rollback on quality regressions. experiments can be tied to prompt sets so you can see degradation against a defined eval.
[04:02] Tom: cost question — what's the typical uplift for dedicated vs hosted per token?
[04:08] Luis: it really depends on utilization. if you commit to reserved capacity, your per-token cost drops significantly because of amortization; hosted is higher per-token but zero ops. we can give indicative numbers in the pricing sheet — i'll attach sample scenarios using your sizing.
[04:24] Sara: for Private deployment, what does network topology look like? can you run entirely inside our VPC with no egress?
[04:31] Luis: private can be VPC-hosted or on-prem. for fully air-gapped we do an on-prem package but that takes longer to stand up (additional weeks for packaging and validation). VPC mode supports no public egress and you can bring your own KMS.
[04:48] Maya: timeline expectations if we do hosted benchmark then dedicated test then private validation — can that fit in 6 weeks?
[04:56] Jamie: approximate plan we recommend: Week 0: onboarding + baseline data & prompts; Week 1–2: hosted benchmark (2 weeks); Week 3: analyze and tune (quantization, batching); Week 4: optional dedicated pool spin-up and benchmark (1 week); Week 5–6: private/VPC validation and security review if needed. so yes— fits 6 weeks but private/on-prem can push beyond depending on procurement.
[05:22] Tom: procurement — what's required for dedicated? are there contracts / minimums?
[05:28] Nina: dedicated typically has a monthly reserved commitment; we can structure a short-term pilot for 2–3 months with a lighter commit. we'll include options in pricing.
[05:40] Devon: benchmark harness — will it be open-source or a link? we prefer to run tests from our infra to reduce network variability.
[05:47] Luis: we'll provide a harness repo link and dockerized runner; ideally run it from a stable host in your VPC to measure end-to-end. for hosted baseline we run from our test cluster and can also run a client in your VPC to measure network delta.
[06:05] Maya: sample load — our peak a few flows per second, bursts to ~20 r/s; typical concurrency ~30 users. we want to ensure tail latency under bursts.
[06:17] Luis: okay that maps to ~1200 r/min spikes. we should size for that with buffer. we'll propose GPU instance types and batch sizes — some heuristics: 8-bit q4_0 etc for Llama-derived models, bf16 for models where accuracy sensitivity is high.
[06:35] Sara: can we control batching policies and latency SLOs? we need deterministic p95 targets.
[06:41] Jamie: yes — you can configure batching thresholds, max latency caps, and have routes with dedicated latency-first policies vs cost-first. we also expose metrics per-token and per-route.
[06:55] Tom: any gotchas on streaming vs non-streaming that affect latency accounting?
[07:02] Luis: streaming reduces Time-to-First-Byte but complicates token accounting for cost. also KV-cache and prefix caching help repeated conversations. we'll surface both real-time and aggregated metrics so you can correlate perceived latency and billed tokens.
[07:22] Maya: what's the typical work for us to get sample prompts into the harness? do you need sanitized production data?
[07:29] Luis: sanitized is ideal. we only need representative token-length distribution and a few hundred to a couple thousand eval prompts for quality checks. for privacy-sensitive content you can use anonymized placeholders.
[07:42] Devon: regarding success criteria, besides latency and cost, we want a quality SLA — e.g., failure modes where model hallucination rate increases. can Redwood detect quality regressions automatically?
[07:53] Jamie: yes — our Eval/Optimize tooling can run regression tests on prompt sets and alert on defined thresholds; you can tie rollback to those alerts during rollouts.
[08:06] Sara: for compliance we need audit logs shipped to our SIEM and retention controls. is that supported?
[08:12] Nina: audit logs, request-level metadata, and configurable retention are available. we can stream logs to your S3 or SIEM endpoint for Private/Dedicated; hosted has export options for enterprise tiers.
[08:26] Tom: curious — any major differences in implementation time between dedicated and private?
[08:33] Luis: dedicated (Redwood Dedicated) is fastest: reserved pools in our infra, a few days to provision after contract; private (VPC) typically takes 1–2 weeks for config and networking; fully on-prem can take 3–6 weeks depending on approvals.
[08:51] Maya: ok. let's talk benchmarks specifics — we'd like p95, p99 at 90/180/360 token lengths. also measure under cold-warm-hot states.
[09:03] Luis: perfect. we'll instrument cold start latency (first request after model load), warm steady-state, and hot burst. we'll also record GPU temps/util to inform autoscaling.
[09:15] Devon: do you have pre-made dashboards for the POC?
[09:19] Nina: yes — we'll provision per-route dashboards including cost/latency breakdowns, token distribution, and regression charts; we'll share links and can embed in your Grafana with our exporter if you prefer.
[09:33] Maya: question on model variants: if a smaller quantized model drops quality by 3% but cuts token cost by 50%, do you recommend autoswitching?
[09:45] Luis: that's a policy decision. Redwood Optimize can recommend tiering — route by SLA: latency first may use quantized variant, quality-first uses full-precision. you can also do A/B to compare real user impact.
[09:58] Tom: on the legal side — any implications around data residency? we need EU-only hosting for some workloads.
[10:05] Jamie: supported — hosted regions include EU/NA/APAC and for strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private in-region. we'll include region-specific notes in the security pack.
[10:18] Maya: ok great. can we capture a short list of success criteria to sign off internally?
[10:23] Jamie: i'll draft an SOC and success criteria doc. from today: (1) p95 < 250ms streaming for chat flows; (2) throughput handle 600 r/min sustained, bursts to 1200 r/min; (3) cost target < $0.015/1k tokens or better with dedicated; (4) quality regression <5% on your eval; (5) security: SOC2, SSO, KMS integration.
[10:45] Devon: helpful. can you also include a test for model drift detection?
[10:50] Luis: yes — we'll include automated evaluation runs daily and regression alerts; you can choose cadence.
[10:58] Maya: a few open Qs: 1) how do you handle customer-managed keys for hosted? 2) what's the lead time to provision a dedicated pool in our preferred region? 3) what's effort to run on-prem later?
[11:12] Luis: (1) hosted + CMK: we have enterprise HSM connectors and can mount your KMS for key wrapping in enterprise accounts; (2) dedicated lead time: typically 3–7 days after contract, depends on region; (3) on-prem: packaging, security validation, and signed binaries — usually 3–6 weeks.
[11:30] Tom: do you provide SLA for latency or just uptime?
[11:35] Jamie: uptime SLA is standard for Dedicated. latency SLOs are configuration-driven; we provide SLO tooling but latency SLAs can be part of enterprise agreements.
[11:45] Sara: will we be able to see per-token billing broken out by route and user?
[11:50] Nina: yes — we expose token-level billing and per-route cost attribution; we can also include per-team breakdowns.
[12:03] Maya: about the benchmark harness — can you show an example of the harness output?
[12:07] Luis: i'll send a sample report — p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost estimate and GPU utilization charts; we'll also include raw CSVs.
[12:18] Devon: regarding the actual POC run — who will operate the dedicated pool if we spin it up?
[12:24] Jamie: Redwood operates Dedicated infra; you get admin controls and we coordinate maintenance windows. for Private on-prem, you'll operate with our ops support.
[12:36] Tom: ok let's cover decision criteria checklist — what would cause us to choose hosted vs dedicated vs private?
[12:44] Luis: my quick checklist:
- Hosted: if you want fastest time-to-value, low ops, and your throughput is moderate; good if no strict residency/KMS requirements.
- Dedicated: if you need predictable unit economics, committed throughput, data isolation, and lower per-token costs at scale.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): if you have strict compliance/residency, require air-gapped/on-prem, or need full control over network and keys.
[13:14] Maya: any middle ground? hybrid?
[13:18] Jamie: yes — start hosted for benchmark then move critical routes to Dedicated and keep other routes on hosted. routing policies and automatic fallback make hybrid practical.
[13:29] Sara: what about SLA and runbook for failover between dedicated and hosted?
[13:33] Luis: we provide failover policies and tracer hooks; we can simulate failover in a test window as part of the POC.
[13:45] Devon: action items recap would be helpful now.
[13:49] Jamie: sure — recapping quickly. Jamie to send pricing/contract + security pack by 11/11; Luis to share harness + sample report by 11/12; Maya to send prompt set & token distribution by 11/13; Sara to confirm VPC/KMS provider by 11/13; schedule hosted benchmark start 11/16.
[14:10] Tom: sounds good. any final questions?
[14:15] Maya: just one — is there any pre-existing Redwood agent or SDK we need to integrate?
[14:21] Luis: we have SDKs for python/node and a simple REST contract; for the harness we recommend using the SDK to collect consistent telemetry.
[14:31] Devon: on quantization, curious if you do post-training quant or proprietary kernels?
[14:36] Luis: mix — we support quantized model versions that are compiled with kernel selection for the runtime; for some sensitive workloads you may prefer bf16 vs q4.0. we'll propose recommendations after we see accuracy tradeoff.
[14:50] Nina: i'll also create a calendar with milestone checkpoints and a slack channel invite.
[14:56] Maya: great. thanks everyone.
[15:00] Jamie: thanks team — we'll follow up with the docs and links.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript had a few word swaps (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate" and "privet" instead of Private), filler words present, and occasional speaker attribution errors (we corrected some during editing).

End of call.
